st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The survey supports the buyer-led reorganisation of legal delivery by documenting procurement-driven consolidation of traditional law-firm rosters alongside growing use of alternative and ancillary providers. Its support is limited: it describes provider allocation and notes that alternative firms were not yet fully mainstream, but does not address AI, time-based pricing, junior training or verification.

kp.k: Survey findings are indicative, not representative
kp.d: The research examines legal procurement rather than AI. It surveyed 153 legal procurement professionals using 33 mostly multiple-choice questions, from mid-December 2017 through early February 2018. Recruitment used emailed links and LinkedIn procurement groups. The report expressly cautions that findings indicate trends rather than representative results, and that changing respondent mixes affect comparisons between surveys.
qs: The survey was completed by 153 legal procurement professionals and comprised 33 mostly multiple-choice questions and focused on purchasing decisions, cost control, analyses, and trends.
The 2018 study was conducted from mid-December 2017 through early February 2018.

Please note that all findings should be seen as indicative, showing trends rather than absolute, representative data due to the sample size in a (still) unknown universe of Legal Procurement professionals.

kp.d: The report argues that management mandates extend beyond reducing expenditure to improving quality and value. It describes a shift among large spenders away from relationship-only purchasing toward active spend management and professional sourcing, and urges providers to respond with better outcomes at lower costs.
qs: The majority of legal spend is now under (some) review and active spend management.
A relationship-only business approach to buying – and selling – legal services is now a small minority among the largest spenders.
It is replaced by a professional, business-driven approach to sourcing.
Winners will respond and deliver better results at lower costs.

kp.k: Respondents report substantial legal spending savings
kp.d: The executive summary reports average savings of 14.6 percent with procurement involvement, compared with 11.4 percent in 2017 in the main text. The main text also separately states a 16.9 percent reduction for 2018 without reconciling it with 14.6 percent. Reported savings include reductions or cost avoidances; the most successful group averaged 20.8 percent, and the highest reported saving was 57 percent.

kp.k: Tenure is associated with procurement effectiveness
kp.d: The report associates longer category tenure with greater savings and self-assessed success. Respondents with 10+ years reported average savings of 19 percent, those with five to nine years 15 percent, and those with two to four years 13 percent. Those with one year or less also reported 15 percent, which the report interprets as possible early quick wins. Success scores for five-to-nine-year and ten-or-more-year groups were 7.25 and 7.41; the report recommends sustained category experience rather than brief rotations.
qs: Quick stints in the legal category are insufficient.
IT TAKES FIVE YEARS TO MASTER THE CATEGORY
SUCCESS IS EARNED WITH TIME IN THE CATEGORY.

kp.k: Internal partnerships accompany higher savings and confidence
kp.d: Respondents describing their relationship with in-house lawyers as partners reported average savings of 21 percent, compared with 15 percent for collegial relationships, 7 percent for reluctant relationships and 9 percent where relationships were absent. Corresponding legal-operations figures were 17, 14 and 10 percent for partner, collegial and reluctant relationships. Positive relationships with law departments rose to 73 percent from 55 percent in 2017; 71 percent reported positive relationships with legal operations. The report advocates collaboration and identifies overlapping vendor-management and analytics responsibilities as potential sources of conflict.

kp.k: Traditional firms dominate spending despite alternative-provider opportunities
kp.d: Respondents reported annual average spending of $113 million with traditional law firms, $5.5 million with alternative legal service providers and $15 million with ancillary providers. Twenty-four percent had not used alternative firms. The smallest organizations, with $26 million to $500 million in revenue, allocated 27 percent of their legal-services budget to alternatives, versus 5 percent among the largest organizations. The report treats greater alternative-provider penetration among large buyers as potential growth, not an established outcome.
qs: LEGAL SPEND: FIVE TIMES MORE ON TRADITIONAL FIRMS THAN OTHER PROVIDERS
ALTERNATIVE LEGAL SERVICES PROVIDERS ARE NOT (YET?) EMBRACED BY ALL ORGANIZATIONS.

kp.k: Traditional firm rosters shrink as alternatives gain traction
kp.d: Across the annual survey samples, the mean number of regularly instructed traditional firms fell from 362 to 149 and the median from 200 to 100; the maximum fell from 1,500 to 900. Mean alternative-firm counts increased from four to six, with medians rising from two to three. Respondents used an average of 25 ancillary providers. The report attributes consolidation to procurement discipline and argues that excessive provider numbers weaken purchasing power, increase administration and inhibit strategic relationships; the methodology cautions that annual samples differ.
qs: ORGANIZATIONS WORK WITH FEWER AND FEWER PROVIDERS.
BUT SOME SAY, THEY STILL WORK WITH TOO MANY.
ALTERNATIVES GAINING TRACTION

kp.k: Procurement combines discounts with analytical and process tools
kp.d: Reported current adoption included discount negotiation at 88 percent, RFPs at 76 percent, sourcing strategies at 75 percent, outside-counsel billing guidelines at 74 percent, panels at 72 percent, eBilling at 69 percent, AFAs at 65 percent and data analytics at 63 percent. Planned adoption was distinct from actual use: 31 percent planned AFAs and 33 percent planned analytics. Respondents with at least five years of experience were more likely to use eAuctions, eBilling, legal project management and analytics.
qs: PROCUREMENT TOOLS USED ARE BECOMING MORE SOPHISTICATED AND INCREASINGLY ANALYTICAL.
Who still pays sticker price?

kp.k: AFAs and scoping outrank discounts in perceived value
kp.d: Respondents identified AFAs, pre-matter scoping and preferred-provider panels as the most valuable tactics; discount negotiation ranked tenth despite widespread use, and eAuctions ranked last. The report recommends developing scoping capabilities, detailed plans, scenarios and budget forecasts. Legal project management was used by 27 percent and planned by 50 percent; scoping was used by 46 percent and planned by 41 percent. These planned uses underpin the report’s growth expectations rather than demonstrate realized adoption.

kp.d: The five leading 2018 goals were better capturing and analyzing spend data, reducing legal expenditure, better management of legal work, implementing formal strategies and processes, and improving law-department relationships. Spend reduction rose from sixth place in the previous survey to second. The report interprets these priorities as increasing sophistication and anticipates greater emphasis on preventing unnecessary work and expenditure rather than relying solely on discounts.
qs: TOP GOALS: BETTER CAPTURE & ANALYZE DATA
PROCUREMENT GOALS SHOW THE INCREASED SOPHISTICATION AND REFINEMENT.
ANALYTICS CONTINUE TO BE ON THE RISE.

kp.k: Expertise and predictability outweigh familiarity and low fees
kp.d: Experience with similar matters was preferred across risk categories, including by 74 percent for high-risk work. Predictability was preferred by 55 percent for high-risk work and 54 percent for complex, significant work; only 2 percent and 3 percent respectively preferred low fees. Routine work differed: 45 percent prioritized low fees, 29 percent efficiency and 26 percent predictability. The report interprets these preferences as opportunities for challengers demonstrating relevant expertise and a warning against incumbents relying on relationships alone.
qs: PREDICTABILITY IS MORE IMPORTANT THAN LOW FEES, UNLESS IT IS FOR ROUTINE WORK.
EXPERIENCE TRUMPS FAMILIARTY.
PREDICTABILITY WINS

kp.k: Clients value free advice access and tailored extras
kp.d: With multiple responses permitted, 63 percent preferred hotlines or access to experts for quick questions, 56 percent seminars and business-level training, and 50 percent secondments. Pre-matter planning sessions attracted 40 percent and provider participation on internal calls 33 percent. The report recommends asking clients which extras they value rather than supplying a standard package; one respondent objected to being charged for everything.

kp.d: Average self-assessed success rose from 5.8 to 6.5 on a ten-point scale. Respondents scoring themselves nine or ten increased from 9 percent to 18 percent; those scoring seven or eight increased from 32 percent to 37 percent. Together these groups represented 55 percent, versus 41 percent previously. However, the least successful group also increased, from 4 percent to 6 percent. These are respondents’ confidence and success assessments, not independent performance evaluations.

kp.d: North American respondents reported higher average savings than Europeans, 15.2 versus 12.4 percent, and higher success scores, 7.01 versus 6.14. European organizations used fewer traditional firms on average, 103 versus 185, but more alternatives, ten versus five. North American adoption was higher for RFPs, eBilling, invoice audits and analytics; eBilling differed particularly sharply at 84 versus 39 percent. The report suggests regional tenure differences may explain some variation and predicts convergence as procurement matures.
qs: LEGAL PROCUREMENT IS NOT THE SAME EVERYWHERE.
AS THE CATEGORY MATURES, THIS MAY CHANGE OVER TIME.
BEST PRACTICES WILL PREVAIL.

kp.k: Maturity framework culminates in collaborative spend management
kp.d: The appendix presents a progression from unmanaged spending at Level 1 to collaborative management at Level 5. Passive management emphasizes policies and self-regulation; active management involves enforcing policies with outside counsel and realizing benefits. Collaborative management adds shared accountability and co-developed solutions among procurement, in-house lawyers and outside counsel. The accompanying matrix recommends prioritizing initiatives by time to benefits, change-management requirements and potential savings, recognizing that suitability varies by organizational culture.
